children: 2000 ET - The Bank of Japan is set to keep its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% this week it assesses the impact of last month's hike, ING economists says. Their base case assumes two additional 25bp hikes in January and April 2027, taking the policy rate to 1.75%. Though inflation remains high, ING reckons policymakers may prefer more time to monitor the economy, particularly as the government continues to support domestic demand. With markets pricing in a hold in October, focus will be on the BOJ's tone and messaging, and on a fresh batch of upcoming economic data. According to ING, consensus is for Tokyo October inflation data to show headline CPI steady year-on-year, and core inflation easing slightly. Nationwide retail sales and industrial production for September are also due. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

1946 ET - Japanese stocks may remain rangebound as concerns about the Iran conflict and higher energy costs continue. Nikkei futures are flat at 62830 on the SGX. The dollar is at 156.85 yen, compared with Y156.93 as of Friday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on any developments in the Middle East and crude oil prices after they hit their highest level in five months on Friday. The Nikkei Stock Average fell 0.3% to 62693.16 on Friday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1943 ET - The Reserve Bank of Australia is now consistently indicating its discomfort about excessive demand in the economy, adding in its public commentary that the situation has to be tackled, says Ivan Colhoun, an economist at Marex. It has also stressed that it must get inflation out of the system and that there are signs inflation is becoming dangerously embedded, Colhoun adds. The RBA's messaging now highlights that the pain of higher inflation is something impacting the entire population, rather than just home buyers, he adds. Colhoun expects an interest rate rise in November.(james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1804 ET - The Reserve Bank of Australia has acknowledged that government spending is contributing to an excess of demand in the economy. The bank's chief economist, Sarah Hunter, said in a television interview that "government spending is part of demand, and it's that imbalance between demand and supply that we're really trying to tackle right now." The comments come ahead of a policy meeting in early November where traders see a strong chance the RBA will deliver a fifth interest rate rise for the year. Last week, the RBA said the inflation outlook had become "materially worse." (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)
